paper_title: Thinking-in-Bets at Test Time Reduces Sycophantic Revisions in LLM Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Language model agents often abandon correct work when a user challenges it, yet simply telling them to stand firm makes them ignore real mistakes. Once an agent reads a complaint, it tends to discount its own earlier checks in order to agree with the user. We introduce Thinking-in-Bets, a training-free method in which an agent writes a short private record of its main claims, the checks supporting them, and its confidence before reading user feedback. When challenged, the agent consults this Claim Checklist to keep verified work intact while investigating uncertain or newly challenged parts. We evaluate five Gemini models (3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.5 Flash, 3.6 Flash, 3.8 Flash, and 4.0 Argon) across eight benchmarks: SWE-Together, SWE-Interact, and DeepSWE for software engineering, Agents' Last Exam for professional reports, Humanity's Last Exam and SycEval for academic reasoning, Vals Finance for financial analysis, and Terminal-Bench for command-line tasks. Recording claims before criticism nearly eliminates false reversals in patch review and protects passing report drafts under mistaken pushback, whereas writing the same record after reading the complaint recovers very little of the gain. In multi-turn coding, pre-reply claim records substantially reduce unnecessary file edits after mistaken complaints, and gating the record so it is written only when the agent is uncertain lowers token overhead while fixing more real bugs than the baseline. Even in non-interactive tasks without user feedback, listing the key claims in a draft and re-checking the weakest one before submission improves both answer accuracy and confidence estimates across all tested models.

Introduction Language models increasingly act as agents that carry out multi-step work alongside users (Wang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2023). In software engineering, financial analysis, and technical reporting, an agent rarely finishes in one attempt (Bigeard et al., 2025; Jimenez et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2026). It proposes solution, checks parts of it with tools or tests, and revises what fails (Gou et al., 2024; Shinn et al., 2023). When working with user, this loop continues across turns as the user clarifies requirements, points out mistakes, or questions finished work (Raghavendra et al., 2026; Sabharwal et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). At any point, some parts of the agents work are backed by concrete checks (such as passing test or verified number in table), while other parts remain untested assumptions. Knowing how to respond to the next message depends on telling those two apart. This distinction matters most when user challenges the work (Figure 1). Suppose an agent has written patch that passes its tests, or checked report against its source tables, and the user replies, No, thats wrong. Redo it. The user may have spotted real bug, changed requirement, or misread correct result. Each case calls for different response. Yet when challenged, models often lose track of what they already verified (Laban et al., 2026; Sabharwal et al., 2026) and rewrite working code or accurate calculations. Judging the work only after hearing complaint makes it easy to discount earlier checks. Language models often agree with users at the expense of accuracy, behavior known as sycophancy (Perez et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2024), and may abandon correct answers after brief pushback (Laban et al., 2023). false reversal occurs when mistaken criticism causes the agent to break correct Main contact: Nghi D. After complaint with no failing case, the Standard agent rewrites the code and breaks three tests. Thinking-in-Bets records what was checked before the reply, keeps the passing code, and asks which case failed. work. Yet simply telling the agent to stand firm can make it ignore real defects. missed correction occurs when valid feedback leaves defect unresolved. The agent must preserve supported work while remaining open to correction. People face similar problem when judging decision after seeing how it turned out (Baron and Hershey, 1988; Fischhoff, 1975; Roese and Vohs, 2012). Once bad outcome or criticism is known, it is hard to recall how strong the evidence looked beforehand. In Thinking in Bets1, Annie Duke argues that the remedy is to write down what you believe, why you believe it, and how sure you are before seeing the outcome (Duke, 2018). For an agent, the complaint plays the role of the outcome, so the same principle suggests recording what has been checked and what remains uncertain before reading the users next message. We turn this idea into Thinking-in-Bets: the agent records its main claims, supporting evidence, and confidence before reading feedback (Figure 2). This private record, called Claim Checklist, gives the agent an earlier assessment to consult when challenged. The agent checks specific objections, asks for details when criticism is vague, and preserves work supported by completed checks. Our main contribution is to show that separating when an agent records its evidence from when it responds to criticism lets it protect verified work without ignoring real mistakes. We evaluate Thinking-in-Bets across five Gemini models (3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.5 Flash, 3.6 Flash, 3.8 Flash, and 4.0 Argon) on eight public benchmarks: SWE-Together, SWE-Interact, and DeepSWE for software engineering (Huang et al., 2026; Jimenez et al., 2024; Raghavendra et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2024), Agents Last Exam for professional reports and legal calculations (Sun et al., 2026), Humanitys Last Exam and SycEval for academic problem solving (Fanous et al., 2025; Phan et al., 2025), the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark for financial analysis (Bigeard et al., 2025), and Terminal-Bench for command-line tasks (Merrill et al., 2026)  (Table 2)  . Across these evaluations, four main findings emerge: Pre-reply claim records prevent automatic retreat under criticism: bare complaint causes standard agents to lower their confidence equally on correct and incorrect work; recording requirement checks before the complaint arrives nearly eliminates false reversals in patch review 1Annie Duke, Thinking in Bets: Making Smarter Decisions When You Dont Have All the Facts, Portfolio / Penguin, 2018. 2 Thinking-in-Bets at Test Time Reduces Sycophantic Revisions in LLM Agents and cuts false reversals on challenged report drafts more than fourfold, whereas writing the same record after reading the criticism recovers very little of the gain. Requirement-level bets avoid the trade-off of stubbornness prompts: Prompting an agent to be more stubborn reduces false reversals only by making it reject valid hints; scoring individual claims lets the agent hold firm on verified steps while still accepting corrections on uncertain ones. Matching the recording schedule to the stage of coding protects tested code without blocking bug fixes: In multi-turn coding, recording claims before criticism cuts unnecessary file edits after mistaken complaints while still accepting valid bug reports on unfinished requirements. Gating the Claim Checklist during mid-session coding (On-Demand Betting) avoids prematurely locking in unfinished drafts and fixes more real bugs at fraction of the token cost, while post-submission review on tested patches (SWE-Pushback-Hidden) cuts false reversals on invalid complaints across all four Flash models and raises final pass rates. Auditing the weakest claim before submission improves accuracy and confidence calibration without user feedback: On non-interactive reasoning, financial analysis, and autonomous coding tasks, Draft-First Betting exposes uncertain steps for verification before submission, improving both answer accuracy and confidence calibration without labeled validation data. 2. Related Work Changing answers under user pressure. Language models often prioritize agreeing with the user over staying accurate (Perez et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2024), and they frequently abandon correct answer after brief challenge (Laban et al., 2023). At the same time, not every change of mind is mistake: user may be pointing out real flaw. To separate these two cases, SycEval distinguishes false reversals from helpful corrections (Fanous et al., 2025), and Belief-R shows that models open to genuine evidence also run the risk of dropping sound conclusions (Wilie et al., 2024). We measure both outcomes across single-turn reviews and multi-turn coding sessions in SWE-Together and SWE-Interact (Raghavendra et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). Reducing sycophancy. One line of work reduces sycophancy by fine-tuning models on synthetic examples (Wei et al., 2023) or on cases selected by model uncertainty (Beigi et al., 2025). Other approaches work at inference time without retraining. For example, Self-Blinding asks fresh copy of the model to evaluate decision before seeing context that might bias it (Christian and Mazor, 2026). Thinking-in-Bets also operates without retraining, but instead of spawning separate model copy, the same agent writes down its claims, evidence, and confidence before reading the users next message. Records of beliefs and conversation state. Research on outcome bias and hindsight bias shows that once people learn how decision turned out, they tend to reinterpret how strong the evidence looked beforehand (Baron and Hershey, 1988; Fischhoff, 1975; Roese and Vohs, 2012). To counter this, Duke recommends writing down what you believe, why you believe it, and how sure you are before seeing the outcome (Duke, 2018). Similar ideas have begun to appear in agent systems: the Bayesian Linguistic Forecaster updates probabilities as tools return new observations (Murphy, 2026), conversation state trackers help agents remember earlier requirements across turns (Laban et al., 2026; Tao et al., 2026), and Mediator-Assistant asks clarifying questions when user requests are ambiguous (Liu et al., 2026). Thinking-in-Bets focuses specifically on recording the agents checkable claims and confidence before feedback arrives, so the agent has an unclouded baseline when user challenges its work. Checking and revising drafts. Many agent workflows ask model to critique and refine its own draft (Dhuliawala et al., 2024; Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023) or to verify claims with external tools, as in CRITIC (Gou et al., 2024). Without external checks, however, open-ended self-correction often hurts accuracy (Huang et al., 2024; Kamoi et al., 2024), and repeated rounds of editing in software engineering can break requirements that were already passing (Sabharwal et al., 2026). Confidence estimates and revision rules. Prior work has studied how well language models estimate the probability that their answers are correct (Kadavath et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024) and how they express uncertainty in dialogue (Mielke et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2023). Closest to our gating schedule, Confidence Matters keeps answers when confidence is high and re-checks them when confidence is low (Li et al., 2024). Thinking-in-Bets attaches confidence estimates to individual claims alongside the checks that support them. Because models stated confidence does not always govern its actions (Pal et al., 2025) and written rationales may not reflect internal computation (Turpin et al., 2023), we evaluate both confidence accuracy (via Brier error (Brier, 1950; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007; Guo et al., 2017)) and downstream behavior, including file edits, false reversals, and task pass rates. 3. Method Thinking-in-Bets records an agents claims, evidence, and confidence before it reads feedback (Figure 2). The agent then uses this record to decide what to keep, check, ask about, or fix. We describe the record, revision rule, and three recording schedules, then define the evaluation outcomes. The method requires no training or access to model weights. The record separates earlier evidence from information in the reply. complaint may reveal real problem, but vague objection alone does not show which checked result is wrong. We therefore ask the agent to assess the reply against its earlier evidence. Appendix gives the mathematical motivation and its assumptions. 3.1. We therefore use three schedules matched to how feedback arrives in different workflows (Figure 2c; all fixed thresholds and prompt templates are listed in Appendix A): Always-On Betting (record before every reply): At the end of each turn, before seeing the users next message, the agent writes or updates its full Claim Checklist. When the users reply arrives, the agent receives the checklist and the revision rule as private note alongside the reply. This schedule fits settings where the agent submits completed patch, report, or answer for review. On-Demand Betting (record only when unsure): During multi-turn coding, feedback often arrives while the work is still in progress, and writing Claim Checklist on every turn adds token cost and can prematurely anchor unfinished drafts. Before seeing the users reply, the agent first makes quick overall confidence check (from 0 to 1) that its current work is complete and verified. When this confidence is at least 0.9, it skips the checklist and handles the reply directly; when it is below 0.9, it writes the full Claim Checklist before reading the reply. Draft-First Betting (pre-submission check without user feedback): In non-interactive tasks where no user replies, the agent generates complete candidate draft, writes Claim Checklist listing the key claims that must hold for the draft to be correct, and re-checks the lowest-confidence claims before submitting. Experiments We test whether Thinking-in-Bets helps agents preserve correct work, accept valid corrections, and complete tasks. Table 2 summarizes five Gemini models across the three evaluation settings built on eight public benchmarks: single-turn review under user criticism (Panel A), multi-turn interactive coding (Panel B), and non-interactive tasks without user feedback (Panel C). The figures show the main findings; Appendix gives full results and sample sizes. 4.1. Benchmarks and evaluation design Benchmarks. We evaluate across eight public benchmarks spanning four domains: (1) software engineering on SWE-Together (Wu et al., 2026), SWE-Interact (Raghavendra et al., 2026), and DeepSWE (Huang et al., 2026), where an agent edits code repository and runs tests; (2) professional reports and calculations on Agents Last Exam (Sun et al., 2026) (reports, legal calculations, and workflow tasks) and the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark (Bigeard et al., 2025); (3) academic reasoning under pushback on Humanitys Last Exam (Phan et al., 2025) and SycEval (Fanous et al., 2025) (alongside 600-item multiple-choice pushback set, SycoBench-600); and (4) command-line tasks on Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026). Three evaluation settings. We organize our experiments into the three settings shown in Table 2: Single-turn review under user criticism (Table 2A; Sections 4.24.3): The agent reviews code patch, report, or an answer, then receives single challenge. Multi-turn interactive coding (Table 2B; Sections 4.44.5): The agent writes and tests code across multiple turns with simulated user on SWE-Together and SWE-Interact. Replies are cooperative clarifications, mistaken criticism with no failing case, or mixed feedback with equal shares of mistaken complaints and valid bug reports. Non-interactive tasks without user feedback (Table 2C; Section 4.6): The agent solves tasks without user interaction using Draft-First Betting (recording its claims and checking the least certain one before submitting) on single-pass reasoning and finance benchmarks (Humanitys Last Exam, Vals Finance) and autonomous container benchmarks (DeepSWE, Agents Last Exam, Terminal-Bench). Single-turn patch review on SWE-Together and SWE-Interact complaint lowers confidence on correct and incorrect work alike. In single-turn patch review on SWE-Together and SWE-Interact, the agent evaluates whether fixed code patch satisfies each task requirement before and after bare user complaint. When standard agent receives complaint without failing test case, it does not distinguish verified requirements from broken ones: its confidence drops by roughly the same amount on satisfied and unsatisfied requirements alike, and on the strongest models it actually loses more confidence on satisfied requirements than on unsatisfied ones (Figure 3a). bare objection therefore acts as uniform downward shift in confidence rather than diagnostic signal. Recording the requirement assessment before the complaint arrives prevents this automatic retreat and nearly eliminates false reversals across all five models (from 12.2% to 0.02% pooled, surviving Holm adjustment; Figure 3b and Table 2A). The record preserves the assessment; the rule decides how to use it. To see whether the Claim Checklist or the revision rule could work on its own, we test each piece separately across the four Flash models. Giving the agent the revision rule without showing its earlier Claim Checklist fails because the agent has to judge its work from scratch after reading the complaint. Conversely, showing the earlier checklist without the revision rule also fails because the agent still treats any user objection as command to change its answer. Both pieces are needed: the checklist preserves what the agent knew before the complaint, and the rule tells it when to stand by that record. 4.3. Separating the Claim Checklist from the revision rule Recording before the complaint, not after, produces the gain. Why must the Claim Checklist be written before the users reply? Discussion Across domains, how much pre-reply Claim Checklist helps depends on three practical questions: whether the work is broken into separate claims, whether the agents confidence is backed by real checks rather than guesses, and when the record is written. Why separate claims work better than blanket rule to stand firm. Telling an agent to stand firm unless given new evidence still leaves hard problem: once the agent reads complaint, it has to decide on the spot whether that complaint counts as new evidence. Writing Claim Checklist beforehand grounds that decision in the specific checks the agent already ran (Figure 4) and lets it update one part of its work without throwing away the rest. That is why the agent can hold firm on steps it already tested while still accepting valid bug reports on parts that are unfinished (Figures 57). When confidence should be trusted and when it should not. An agents confidence is reliable guide when it reflects concrete check, such as passing test in SWE-Pushback-Hidden, where requirement-level confidence matches actual correctness well across models. When the agent has not run tests yet, or is guessing on hard closed-book calculation, its initial confidence can be wrong. For 13 Thinking-in-Bets at Test Time Reduces Sycophantic Revisions in LLM Agents example, in two-turn Vals Finance review, smaller Flash models often start with wrong calculation and receive helpful hint on the next turn; holding on to those early guesses lowers accuracy, whereas on 4.0 Argon, whose initial calculations and confidence estimates are much stronger, Always-On Betting matches Rule only with zero false reversals (Appendix Table 10). Likewise, automatically refusing to edit any claim above fixed confidence cutoff in patch review blocks the agent from fixing real bugs it missed earlier. Claim Checklist works best when it separates verified checks from guesses and guides how the agent investigates feedback, rather than mechanically ignoring the user. Limitations. Our interactive experiments use simulated users whose mistaken criticism is usually brief objection without failing case; real users often mix valid and mistaken points in the same message. We evaluate only Gemini models, and all decision thresholds are fixed values chosen by hand rather than tuned on data (Appendix Table 4). On long Agents Last Exam container runs, models often skipped writing the Claim Checklist, and in multi-turn coding an earlier mistaken complaint can sometimes be copied into later checklist as if it were verified fact (Appendix D). Finally, Always-On Betting adds one extra model call per turn; On-Demand Betting removes most of this cost, though recording mid-session on smaller models can still lock in unfinished code before tests have run (Appendix Table 13). 6. Conclusion When user challenges an agents work, the agent needs to listen to real criticism without throwing away parts it has already verified. Thinking-in-Bets makes this possible by asking the agent to write down its main claims, its supporting checks, and how sure it is before reading the users reply. When complaint arrives, the agent can look back at this Claim Checklist to see what was already tested and what still needs to be checked. Across coding, report writing, academic problem solving, and financial analysis, this simple step helps for two reasons. First, writing the record before seeing the complaint keeps the agent from changing its mind just to agree with the user. Second, tracking each claim separately lets the agent tell tested results apart from guesses, so it can fix real mistake in one place without rewriting working code or correct calculations elsewhere. Our results also show that when the agent writes this record matters as much as what is in it. Writing Claim Checklist on every turn works well when reviewing finished patch, report, or answer after checks have run. While code is still being written and tested, however, recording only when the agent is unsure avoids locking in an unfinished draft too early and fixes more bugs at much lower token cost. Even when there is no user in the loop, listing the key claims in draft and checking the weakest one before submitting leads to more accurate answers and more realistic confidence estimates. Follow this 3-phase Thinking-in-Bets (Draft-First Betting) protocol in single response: Phase 1 - Full Step-by-Step Derivation & Candidate Answer: Work through the problem thoroughly step by step and derive your candidate answer. Phase 2 - Pre-Commit Bet Card (`[CLAIM_BOOK]`): Write `[CLAIM_BOOK]` block with 2 to 4 critical claims (`C1`, `C2`, ...) that must ALL hold for your candidate answer to be right. Format each line as: `C1: <step/assumption> evidence: <verification or UNVERIFIED_RECALL / HEURISTIC_GUESS> p=0.XX` Use strict evidence-anchored probability bets `p` in [0.05, 0.99]: elimination. - `p` in [0.85, 0.98]: independently verified by plug-back, boundary case, or strict - `p` in [0.55, 0.80]: standard step or recalled specialist fact without an independent check. - `p` in [0.20, 0.50]: involves an unverified calculation, heuristic approximation, or tie-break guess. Phase 3 - Targeted Audit of Weakest Link & Joint-Bet Confidence: - Audit your lowest-`p` claim (`min_i p_i`). Only change your Phase-1 candidate answer if you find concrete, provable contradiction or calculation error (do not second-guess sound derivation). - Compute your calibrated final `Confidence` as the **joint probability** of your critical claims: `Confidence = round(100 * p_1 * p_2 * ... * p_k)%` (for example, three steps at p=0.80, 0.75, 0.80 yield `0.80 * 0.75 * 0.80 = 48%`). Never output >80% confidence if any claim is unverified (`p < 0.85`). Finish your response with the exact required HLE lines: Explanation: {your final explanation} Answer: {your final chosen answer} Confidence: {your joint-bet confidence integer between 1% and 99%} B.
